4120:
To demand something means to ask for it in a firm, forceful, non-negotiable way — as if you have the right to receive it and you expect it to happen without question. It is much stronger than simply "asking."

Think of it this way: if you ask someone to return your money, you are being polite, and they could refuse. If you demand it back, you are insisting on it — you are making clear that you believe you are entitled to it and that refusal is not truly an acceptable option.

1. A person demands something

This is the most common use. A person — or a group — makes a forceful request, usually from a place of authority, strong emotion, or a sense of rightful entitlement.

  • The workers demanded higher wages.
  • She demanded an apology from him.
  • The customer demanded to speak to the manager.
  • He burst into the room and demanded to know who had taken his files.
  • The rebels demanded the release of all political prisoners.

In every one of these, the person doing the demanding is asserting that they have a right to what they want. They are not politely hoping for it — they expect it.

2. A situation or thing "demands" something

Here, the subject is not a person but a task, a situation, a circumstance, or a quality. In this sense, "demand" means to require — to make something absolutely necessary. There is no personality or emotion here, just a strong sense of: without this, it cannot work.

  • This job demands complete honesty.
  • Learning a language demands patience and time.
  • The crisis demanded immediate action.
  • Running a marathon demands both physical and mental strength.
  • Great art demands great effort.

The meaning is: this thing is not optional — it is genuinely necessary.

When a person demands something, the tone is usually one of these:

  • Authority — someone with power over others (a boss, a judge, a commanding officer) is ordering that something happen.
  • Anger or frustration — someone who feels wronged and wants a remedy, now.
  • Urgency — something needs to happen immediately and there is no time for politeness.
  • Entitlement — the speaker firmly believes they have a right that is being withheld or ignored.

Because of this, "demanding" can sometimes sound rude or aggressive depending on the situation. Someone demanding help at the scene of an accident is completely understandable. Someone demanding first-class service at a diner as though they are royalty comes across as arrogant. The word carries that weight, and you feel it in context.

Here are the four main grammatical structures you'll encounter:

1. demand + noun

She demanded an explanation.
The general demanded unconditional surrender.

2. demand + to + verb

He demanded to see the evidence.
She demanded to be heard.

3. demand + that + clause

The judge demanded that the witness tell the truth.
They demanded that the company pay compensation.

(Important note: after "demand that," English typically uses the base form of the verb — "tell," not "tells" or "told." This is called the subjunctive mood, and it's standard in formal English.)

4. demand + question word + clause

She demanded to know why it had happened.
He demanded to know who was responsible.
How It Differs from Similar Words

WordWhat it meansTone
AskMake a request, openly and politelyGentle; the other person can easily say no
RequestMake a formal, polite appealRespectful; refusal is still possible
InsistHold firmly to your positionPersistent; about not backing down
DemandFirmly assert your right to somethingForceful; expects compliance; strongest of these

(When used of situations rather than people, "demand" is stronger and more urgent than "require," though both express necessity.)

• The union demanded better safety conditions at the factory. (Workers asserting this as their right — not asking as a favour.)
  • He grabbed the officer's arm and demanded to be released at once. (Forceful, urgent, emotional.)
  • The role of a surgeon demands years of rigorous training. (Without it, the role is simply impossible.)
  • The teacher demanded silence. (Authority — she was not asking; she expected it.)
  • The situation demanded a difficult but honest conversation. (The circumstances made it necessary — not optional.)
  • Protesters gathered outside and demanded answers. (A collective, forceful call for accountability.)

Do not use "demand" for normal, everyday requests. If you ask a colleague to send you a file, you "ask" — you do not "demand." If you tell a friend you'd love to try that restaurant they mentioned, you're "suggesting" or "expressing interest" — not demanding.

Reserve "demand" for moments when:

  • there is real force, urgency, or strong emotion behind the request,
  • someone is asserting a right or authority,
  • or a situation genuinely requires something without which it cannot proceed.

Using "demand" for minor, everyday situations will make you sound unnecessarily aggressive or out of place.

"Demand" always carries a sense of non-negotiable necessity — whether it comes from a person who believes they have the right to something, or from a situation that simply cannot function without a particular thing. The word is never passive, never soft, and never leaves much room for "no."
4121:
To demarcate something means to clearly establish and mark where one thing ends and another begins — to draw a firm, deliberate line that separates two things from each other.

Think of it this way: imagine you and your neighbor share a large open field with no fence. One day, you both agree on exactly where your land ends and theirs begins, and you drive a row of stakes into the ground along that agreed line. You have just demarcated the boundary. The act of intentionally setting and marking that dividing line — that is demarcating.
The most important quality of this word

Demarcation is always deliberate and purposeful. This is what makes "demarcate" more precise than everyday words like "separate" or "divide." Things can separate or divide naturally — a river divides two towns, rain separates the dry ground from the wet. But you don't accidentally demarcate something. Someone consciously decides where the line goes and makes it clear.

So a river might divide two countries naturally, but a government demarcates the official border between them — by a conscious decision, drawn on a map, marked on the ground.

Physical demarcating involves real, visible markers in the world — a painted line on a road, a fence around a property, a sign at the edge of a construction zone, flags along a border. The line you can see or touch is the result of demarcating.

Abstract demarcating involves drawing a clear line between ideas, roles, time periods, disciplines, or responsibilities — where no physical line exists, but the distinction is made sharp and deliberate. A contract, for example, can demarcate exactly which tasks belong to one team and which belong to another. A definition can demarcate where one concept ends and another begins.

Physical use:

  • "The stone wall demarcates the farmland from the public road."
  • "A red line demarcates the safe zone from the restricted area."
  • "The river has historically demarcated the border between the two nations."

Abstract use:

  • "The agreement clearly demarcates each partner's responsibilities."
  • "It is genuinely difficult to demarcate where art ends and science begins."
  • "The new policy demarcates the roles of local and national government."

"Demarcate" is a formal word. You will encounter it most often in legal documents, official agreements, academic writing, journalism about borders or policy, and professional settings. In casual conversation, people tend to say "draw the line," "mark off," "define," or "separate" instead. That said, using "demarcate" in speech isn't wrong — it just sounds precise and authoritative.
How it compares to similar words

Delimit is the closest synonym — it also means to fix the limits of something, and is often used for abstract limits. The two words are nearly interchangeable in many contexts, though "demarcate" often carries a stronger sense of physically marking or visually establishing a boundary.

Delineate overlaps somewhat, but it also means to describe or portray something clearly, not just to divide it. You delineate a plan; you demarcate a boundary.

Distinguish means to notice or point out differences between things — it is about recognizing difference, not about drawing a firm line of separation.

Define is broader — it means to state what something is. Demarcating is a specific kind of defining: the kind where you set its outer edges.

None of these perfectly replaces "demarcate" in all contexts, because demarcate uniquely combines deliberate action + clear boundary-setting into a single precise idea.

In real writing, you will often see: demarcate a boundary, demarcate a border, demarcate zones, demarcate roles, demarcate responsibilities, demarcate areas, clearly demarcated, well-demarcated, sharply demarcated. When something is described as "clearly demarcated" or "well-demarcated," it means its boundaries are obvious, crisp, and easy to identify.

The verb "demarcate" describes the action — the act of drawing the line. The related noun, demarcation, refers to the result — the line or boundary itself that was established.

So: "They demarcated the zones" means they performed the act. "The demarcation of the zones" refers to the resulting division. You'll see both words used often together in the same contexts — borders, responsibilities, scientific fields, safety regulations.
The complete picture in one sentence

To demarcate is to deliberately and clearly establish where one thing ends and another begins — whether that line is drawn on physical ground or between ideas, roles, or concepts — making a distinction that is firm, intentional, and recognizable.
4122:
Demarcation means the action of drawing a clear line to separate two things, or the line itself that separates them.

Think of it this way: imagine you and your sibling share a bedroom. One day, you draw an actual line down the middle of the floor and say, "Your side. My side." That line — and the act of drawing it — is demarcation.

It answers the question: "Where does one thing end and another begin?"
The Two Sides of the Word

Demarcation carries two closely related meanings that work together:

1. The act of establishing a boundary or limit
This is demarcation as a process — the deliberate effort to define, clarify, or establish where one thing stops and another starts.

The committee was responsible for the demarcation of the country's northern border.

Here, demarcation is the work of drawing the border.

2. The boundary or dividing line itself
This is demarcation as a result — the actual line, limit, or distinction that exists after that process.

The river served as a natural demarcation between the two regions.

Here, demarcation is the line — the river is that dividing marker.
It Works for Physical AND Abstract Things

This is important: demarcation doesn't only refer to physical lines on maps or land. It is used just as often — perhaps even more often — to describe invisible, conceptual boundaries.

Physical examples:

  • The demarcation of a country's borders after a war.
  • A fence that acts as a demarcation between two properties.
  • A yellow line on the floor of a factory as a demarcation between the safe zone and the dangerous machinery area.

Abstract/conceptual examples:

  • The demarcation between what is legal and what is illegal.
  • A clear demarcation between a doctor's responsibilities and a nurse's responsibilities.
  • The blurry demarcation between being a friend and being a romantic partner.
  • The demarcation between art and entertainment — where does one end and the other begin?

In every case, the word is doing the same job: it points to a line, limit, or distinction that separates two different things, roles, spaces, or ideas.
Sharpening Your Understanding: What Makes Demarcation Special

The word "demarcation" is stronger and more precise than simply saying "difference" or "separation." Here's why:

  • A difference is passive — it just exists naturally.
  • A demarcation is active and deliberate — it implies that someone has drawn, defined, or enforced a boundary, or that a distinct line clearly exists.

If you say "there is a difference between science and religion," you're just noting two things aren't the same. But if you say "there is a clear demarcation between science and religion," you're saying a specific, identifiable dividing line has been drawn (or is being drawn) between them.

Demarcation implies clarity, deliberateness, and definition.
The Most Common Phrases You'll Encounter

Clear demarcation — when the boundary between two things is obvious and well-defined.

There is a clear demarcation between the roles of the president and the prime minister in this system.

Demarcation line — the actual dividing line itself, often used in political or military contexts.

The ceasefire agreement established a demarcation line that neither army could cross.

Demarcation dispute — a conflict (often between workers or unions) about who has the right to do a particular task or own a particular role.

The factory came to a standstill because of a demarcation dispute between the electricians and the engineers over who should install the new equipment.

Blurred/blurry demarcation — when the boundary between two things is unclear or hard to define.

Modern technology has created a blurred demarcation between work life and personal life.

No clear demarcation — when no obvious dividing line exists.

In her writing, there is no clear demarcation between memoir and fiction.

To confirm you've truly grasped it, read these two sentences:

  • "The demarcation of responsibilities was poorly handled — nobody knew who was in charge of what."
    → The act of defining/assigning clear roles was done badly.
  • "The stone wall formed a demarcation between the ancient city and the forest beyond it."
    → The wall itself is the boundary, the dividing line.

Both are correct uses of the same word. In the first, it's the process. In the second, it's the result.

Demarcation = the act of drawing a clear boundary between two things, or the boundary itself — whether that boundary is physical (a border, a line, a wall) or abstract (between roles, ideas, disciplines, or concepts).
4123:
To demean someone means to treat them in a way that lowers their dignity, worth, or self-respect — to make them feel small, inferior, or unworthy of basic respect. When you demean someone, you are essentially stripping away their dignity, either through your words, actions, or the way you treat them.

Think of dignity as something like a crown a person wears. To demean someone is to knock that crown off their head — to reduce them in a way that feels humiliating or degrading.

This is one of the most important things to understand about this word. You can demean someone else, or you can demean yourself.

Demeaning another person means treating them disrespectfully in a way that damages how they feel about their own worth.

"The boss demeaned his workers by speaking to them as if they were stupid."
"That advertisement demeans women by treating them as objects."

Demeaning yourself (the reflexive use) means doing something that lowers your own dignity — acting beneath your own standards, values, or self-worth. This form is extremely common.

"I refuse to demean myself by begging for his approval."
"She felt she was demeaning herself by staying silent while he insulted her."

When used reflexively like this, there is often a sense of choosing not to lower yourself — people use it to assert their self-respect.

The act of demeaning is not always about loud, obvious insults. It can be subtle. Anything that treats a person as less worthy, less capable, or less important than they are can be demeaning. This includes:

  • Speaking down to someone condescendingly (as if they are a child)
  • Assigning someone a task that is beneath their role or dignity
  • Mocking someone publicly
  • Ignoring someone's opinion consistently as if it doesn't matter
  • Making someone feel ashamed of who they are

The key idea is always the loss of dignity and respect.

The word is very frequently used as an adjective — demeaning — to describe something that causes this loss of dignity.

"She found it demeaning to be asked to fetch coffee when she was a senior engineer."
"The working conditions were demeaning and unfair."
"He was forced into a demeaning situation by his cruel classmates."

When you call something "demeaning," you are saying that it has the quality of stripping away someone's dignity. This form is arguably even more common in everyday speech than the verb itself.
How It Differs from Similar Words

Several words are close in meaning, but each has a slightly different focus. Understanding these differences will sharpen your understanding of "demean."

Humiliate focuses on the emotion — making someone feel intense shame or embarrassment, often publicly. Humiliation is more about the crushing feeling. Demeaning is broader — you can demean someone quietly, without them even reacting visibly.

Belittle means to make someone feel that they and their abilities are small and unimportant. Belittling is mostly done through words and comparisons. Demeaning is wider — it covers actions and treatment, not just words.

Degrade is the closest word to "demean." To degrade also means to lower someone's dignity or worth. The difference is subtle: degrade often implies a deeper, more severe lowering, or is used in more serious, formal contexts (such as "degrading treatment" in human rights language). Demean is slightly softer and is used in everyday situations too.

Disrespect is a broad umbrella word. You can disrespect someone without demeaning them. For example, arriving late to a meeting is disrespectful, but it doesn't necessarily demean anyone. Demeaning always involves an attack on dignity and self-worth specifically.
A Less Common, Older Meaning (Worth Knowing)

In older or very formal literary English, "demean" was also used to mean to conduct or behave oneself — similar to how we use the word "demeanor" today. You might come across a sentence like:

"He demeaned himself with great dignity throughout the trial."

Here it means "he conducted himself" or "he carried himself." This usage is now rare and largely archaic. You are extremely unlikely to encounter it in modern writing or conversation, but if you do come across it in older texts, don't be confused — the context will make it clear.

To demean is to lower someone's dignity and self-worth through your words, actions, or treatment of them. It can be directed at others or at yourself. The related adjective demeaning describes anything that carries this quality of stripping away respect and dignity. It sits in a family of words — humiliate, belittle, degrade — but its specific focus is on the lowering of a person's dignity and sense of worth, whether that happens loudly or quietly, in public or in private.
4124:
If something is demeaning, it lowers a person's dignity — it makes them feel small, worthless, disrespected, or less than human. It strips away a person's sense of self-worth, either in their own eyes, in the eyes of others, or both.

Think of it this way: every person carries an invisible sense of value and respect — a kind of inner dignity. Something demeaning attacks that dignity. It chips away at it, crushes it, or dismisses it entirely.
Breaking It Down Simply

Imagine you are a capable, intelligent adult. Now imagine your boss asks you, in front of your entire team, to pick up their trash from the floor — not because it's your job, but simply to show everyone that they have power over you. That task, in that context, is demeaning. It's not just unpleasant. It sends a message: "You are beneath me. You are not worthy of respect."

That is the heart of the word. Something demeaning doesn't just make you feel bad — it reduces your worth as a person, or at least tries to.
What Kinds of Things Can Be "Demeaning"?

The adjective "demeaning" can describe:

1. Tasks or work
When a task is designed or used — intentionally or not — to make someone feel inferior or unimportant. Example: "He refused to do the demeaning chores that were clearly meant to humiliate him."

2. Language or words
When words or comments suggest that a person is stupid, worthless, inferior, or not deserving of respect. Example: "Her demeaning remarks made the new employee feel unwelcome and worthless."

3. Treatment or behaviour
When a person is treated in a way that strips them of their dignity. Example: "Being searched in public like a criminal felt deeply demeaning."

4. Situations or conditions
When a situation, system, or circumstance reduces a person's dignity. Example: "Living in those conditions was demeaning — they were not treated as human beings."
The Key Ingredient: Dignity

Understanding "demeaning" properly means understanding dignity. Dignity is your basic human worth — the respect you deserve simply because you are a person. It's the feeling that you matter, that you are valued, that you are not "less than" others.

Something demeaning attacks this. It could be:

  • A look that says "you're stupid"
  • A tone of voice that says "you don't matter"
  • A task that says "you're my servant, not my equal"
  • A condition that says "you are not worthy of basic respect"

The attack on dignity is what separates "demeaning" from simply "unpleasant" or "difficult."
Intent vs. Effect — An Important Nuance

Here is something many learners miss: something can be demeaning even if the person doing it didn't mean to be cruel.

  • A doctor who explains a diagnosis to a patient using overly simple language — as if the patient is a child — may not intend to insult them. But the patient can rightly find it demeaning, because it implies they are not intelligent enough to handle real information.
  • A manager who constantly re-checks a senior employee's basic work, even though the employee is highly experienced, may not realise they are being insulting. But the employee can reasonably feel the behaviour is demeaning, because it signals a lack of trust and respect.

So the word "demeaning" focuses on the effect on the person's dignity, not necessarily on the other person's evil intent.

That said — demeaning treatment is very often deliberate. People in positions of power sometimes use demeaning behaviour as a tool to control others or to remind others of their lower status.
Degree and Intensity

"Demeaning" is not a mild word. It sits toward the stronger end of the scale. Compare:

  • Rude — disrespectful in manner
  • Disrespectful — failing to show proper respect
  • Condescending — treating someone as if they are inferior or less intelligent
  • Demeaning — actively reducing a person's dignity and worth ← stronger
  • Degrading — extremely demeaning; reducing a person almost to the level of an object ← even stronger, and often used in extreme or formal contexts

"Demeaning" and "degrading" are very close in meaning, but "degrading" tends to suggest a more extreme or humiliating reduction of a person's dignity (you will often see "degrading treatment" used in human rights contexts). "Demeaning" is the broader, more everyday word.
How It Feels From the Inside

If you experience something demeaning, you are likely to feel:

  • Humiliated
  • Belittled
  • Disrespected
  • Ashamed (even though you've done nothing wrong)
  • Angry, because you know your worth is being dismissed

This emotional response — the feeling of having your worth dismissed or attacked — is one of the clearest signs that something is, in fact, demeaning.
Words That Mean Something Similar

• Belittling — making someone feel small and unimportant
  • Humiliating — causing deep embarrassment and loss of dignity, often in front of others
  • Degrading — lowering someone to a lesser or base level; similar to demeaning but stronger
  • Condescending — treating someone as if they are not as intelligent or capable as you
  • Dehumanising — treating someone as though they are not fully human

All of these words share the idea of reducing a person's dignity. "Demeaning" is the clean, clear, widely-used term that fits most everyday situations.
Words That Mean the Opposite

• Respectful — treating someone with the dignity they deserve
  • Honouring — actively recognising someone's worth and value
  • Uplifting — raising someone's sense of self-worth
  • Dignifying — treating someone in a way that affirms their worth
Common Sentence Patterns

You will very often see "demeaning" used in these patterns:

  • "It is demeaning to..." — e.g., "It is demeaning to ask someone to beg for basic necessities."
  • "...found it demeaning" — e.g., "She found the uniform deeply demeaning."
  • "a demeaning experience/comment/task/remark/treatment"
  • "demeaning to women / to workers / to prisoners" — specifying who is being demeaned
One-Sentence Summary

Demeaning describes anything — a word, action, task, or situation — that lowers a person's dignity and makes them feel worthless, inferior, or disrespected, as though they do not deserve to be treated as a full and valued human being.
4125:
Demeanor is the overall impression a person gives to others through the way they outwardly carry themselves — their behavior, body language, facial expressions, tone of voice, and general attitude, all taken together.

It is the "package" of signals you send to the world around you, consciously or not, that tells people what kind of person you seem to be — or how you are feeling — in a given moment or in general.

Think of it this way: if you walked into a room right now, before you said a single word, people would already be forming an impression of you. Are you standing tall or hunched? Do you look calm or nervous? Is your face warm and open, or cold and closed off? Do you move with confidence or hesitation? All of that, together, is your demeanor.
What Makes Up a Person's Demeanor

Demeanor is not one single thing. It is a combination of several outward signals:

Facial expressions — Are they smiling, frowning, or expressionless? Do they look interested or bored?

Body language and posture — Do they stand tall and open, or are they slouched and withdrawn?

Tone of voice — Do they speak gently, harshly, nervously, or calmly? (Note: the words they say are not the demeanor — it's how they say them.)

The way they act and move — Are they restless and anxious, or relaxed and composed? Approachable or standoffish?

Their general attitude as it shows outwardly — Do they come across as friendly, aggressive, professional, threatening, or welcoming?

Demeanor is everything you observe about a person before — or even while — you hear what they are actually saying.
A Crucial Distinction: Outward vs. Inward

This is the most important thing to understand about demeanor: it is always outward. It is about what others can see and sense about you, not about what is happening inside you.

A person might be absolutely terrified on the inside, but if they stand straight, speak calmly, and keep their expressions steady, their demeanor is calm and composed. Conversely, someone might feel perfectly fine internally but come across as hostile or unapproachable because of how they carry themselves.

This is why demeanor matters so much — people judge and respond to your demeanor even when they cannot know your true inner feelings.
Demeanor Can Be General or Situational

Demeanor works on two levels:

General/habitual demeanor — This is how a person typically comes across. Some people have a naturally warm demeanor — they always seem approachable and kind. Others have a stern or serious demeanor by default.

For example: "She had a calm and gentle demeanor that made everyone around her feel at ease."

Situational demeanor — This is how a person carries themselves in a specific situation, which might differ from their usual self.

For example: "Despite the chaos around him, his demeanor remained surprisingly composed."
Demeanor Can Be Positive or Negative

Demeanor is a neutral word — it doesn't mean good or bad by itself. It simply describes how someone comes across. The quality is added by the describing word (adjective) used with it.

Positive demeanor: calm, warm, professional, friendly, confident, polite, cheerful, composed, reassuring.

Negative demeanor: hostile, aggressive, cold, nervous, arrogant, dismissive, threatening, rude, erratic.

Neutral demeanor: quiet, reserved, serious, formal, stoic.

Demeanor is almost always used with a describing word (adjective) that tells you what kind of demeanor is being discussed. You rarely hear the word used alone. Some natural examples:

  • "The suspect's demeanor during questioning made the detective suspicious."
  • "Her calm demeanor helped the frightened child relax."
  • "He maintained a professional demeanor throughout the meeting, even when things got heated."
  • "The teacher's stern demeanor kept the students from misbehaving."
  • "There was something unsettling about his demeanor — he seemed too relaxed for someone in that situation."

You will also notice demeanor is often commented on when it is surprising or noteworthy — when the way someone carries themselves either matches or contradicts what you might expect given the situation.
How Demeanor Differs From Similar Words

These words are often confused with demeanor, so understanding the difference sharpens your grasp of the word.

Personality is who you are on the inside — your inner traits, values, and character. Demeanor is how those (or any feelings) show up on the outside. Personality is internal; demeanor is external.

Behavior refers to specific, individual actions — what you do. Demeanor is broader and more holistic — it's the overall impression created by how you do everything, not just one action.

Attitude is your inner mental or emotional stance toward something (positive attitude, negative attitude). Demeanor is how that attitude — or any emotional state — appears to other people outwardly.

Manner (or manners) is more about specific social habits — how you greet people, how you eat, how polite you are in particular acts. Demeanor is the bigger, overall picture that includes manner but goes beyond it.
Why This Word Matters in Real Life

Demeanor carries significant weight in many real-world situations:

In professional settings, a calm and confident demeanor can earn trust, while a sloppy or dismissive demeanor can damage credibility — even if your actual work is excellent.

In legal settings, a witness's or defendant's demeanor in court is carefully observed — it influences how believable or trustworthy they appear to judges and juries.

In healthcare, a doctor's warm and reassuring demeanor can make a patient feel safe and cared for, while a cold or rushed demeanor can make the patient feel ignored — regardless of the quality of treatment.

In social life, demeanor is often the first thing that draws people toward you or pushes them away, before they even know anything real about you.

If you had to distill it to a single sentence: demeanor is the way a person comes across to others through everything about their outward behavior and bearing — their expressions, posture, tone, and manner — giving people an overall impression of who they are or how they feel.
4126:
Demented means having a severely disturbed or broken-down mind — a mind that has lost its grip on reality, reason, or normal functioning. Think of it as a mind that is no longer working the way a healthy mind should.

But here's the important thing: demented has two distinct lives — one in serious, literal use, and one in everyday casual use. You need to know both to truly master this word.

In its literal sense, demented describes a person who is suffering from dementia — a medical condition where the brain deteriorates, usually in old age, causing severe loss of memory, clear thinking, and the ability to function normally.

A person who is demented in this sense:

  • Cannot remember basic things, even who their family members are
  • May not know where they are or what year it is
  • May behave in confused, erratic, or distressing ways
  • Has permanently and seriously lost mental capacity

Examples:

  • "The demented patient could no longer recognize his own children."
  • "Caring for a demented elderly parent is emotionally exhausting."

This is a grave, clinical use of the word. It describes real suffering, real disease, and real loss of mental function. It is not a casual or light-hearted usage. In fact, many medical professionals and caregivers today consider calling a person "demented" to be somewhat harsh and dehumanizing, preferring instead to say someone "has dementia" or is "living with dementia." So be careful when using this sense — it carries weight.

This is the sense you will encounter far more often in day-to-day conversation, books, and media. In casual use, demented means wildly irrational, frantically crazy, or completely out of control — but not in a medical way. It is used to vividly describe behavior, energy, or ideas that seem extreme, chaotic, or unhinged.

Here, no one is actually claiming the person has a brain disease. The word is being used expressively and often hyperbolically (meaning with exaggeration for effect) to say: "This behavior or situation is so extreme, so uncontrolled, so beyond reason, that it looks insane."

Examples:

  • "She was rushing around the kitchen like a demented person, trying to cook for thirty guests." → Frantically chaotic, not literally ill.
  • "The fans cheered with demented enthusiasm." → Wild, unrestrained, almost frightening in its intensity.
  • "He has some truly demented ideas about how to run a business." → Ideas that seem so bizarre and irrational they appear crazy.
  • "You'd have to be demented to jump off that cliff." → You'd have to be wildly, irrationally reckless.
  • "The comedian had a demented sense of humour." → Weird, dark, twisted in an entertaining way.

In this sense, demented often carries a tone of amused disbelief, exasperation, or even affectionate amusement. When someone says you have a "demented sense of humour," they might actually mean it as a compliment — your humour is delightfully bizarre.

Demented is never a neutral word. It always carries intensity. Depending on context:

  • In the literal sense, it is sorrowful, serious, and heavy. It evokes sympathy and gravity.
  • In the informal sense, it is vivid, expressive, and punchy. It often conveys shock, exasperation, or dark humor.

It is stronger than words like "confused" or "odd." If you say someone is confused, it is mild. If you say someone is demented, you are saying things have gone far beyond normal — into territory that seems broken, chaotic, or extreme.
How to Tell Which Sense Is Being Used

The context always makes it clear.

  • If the sentence is talking about an elderly person, a hospital, memory loss, or cognitive decline → literal medical sense.
  • If the sentence is describing wild behavior, crazy energy, bizarre ideas, or extreme actions in a casual way → informal expressive sense.

You will almost never be confused between the two once you see the surrounding words.

• It does not mean temporarily angry or upset. If someone loses their temper for a moment, you would not call them demented.
  • It does not simply mean eccentric or unusual. An eccentric person is quirky but harmless and in control. A demented person (in the informal sense) seems wildly out of control.
  • It does not mean evil or wicked. A villain is not demented just for being cruel — demented specifically implies irrationality, chaos, or a broken connection to reason.
Words That Are Similar — and How They Differ

Understanding demented alongside similar words sharpens your understanding of all of them.

  • Crazy / Mad: Very close to the informal sense of demented, but more general and milder. Demented is more vivid and dramatic — it suggests something more intense and unhinged than just "crazy."
  • Insane: Also very close, but insane is often used more broadly (about situations, decisions, prices, etc.). Demented tends to focus more specifically on behavior or the mind.
  • Frenzied: Describes wild, uncontrolled action. Similar to demented in energy, but frenzied is about speed and frenzy, while demented adds the flavor of irrationality and mental chaos.
  • Delirious: Means confused and not thinking clearly, often due to fever or extreme emotion. Delirium is temporary and often physical in cause. Demented implies something deeper and more fundamental is broken.
  • Unhinged: Very similar to demented in the informal sense — both suggest a mind that has "come loose" from reason. Unhinged, however, often suggests a sudden snapping point (a person who suddenly became unstable), while demented can describe a more constant, ongoing state of wildness or chaos.

• ✅ "The crowd was demented with excitement, surging and screaming beyond all control."
  • ✅ "It's a demented plan — it makes absolutely no rational sense."
  • ✅ "The film is a demented comedy full of bizarre twists."
  • ✅ "He drove with demented speed through the narrow streets."
  • ⚠️ Avoid casually calling a real person with dementia "demented" in conversation — opt for "living with dementia" instead, as it is more respectful.

Demented means either (1) genuinely suffering from severe mental deterioration due to a brain disease like dementia, or (2) behaving in a wildly irrational, frantic, or chaotic way — beyond all normal reason or control. It is always an intense word, never mild, and always signals that something has gone far beyond what a sound, rational mind would do or experience.

Dementia is not the name of a single disease. It is an umbrella term — a broad, general label — used to describe a serious, ongoing decline in a person's mental abilities that is severe enough to interfere with their daily life.

Think of it this way: just as the word "fruit" covers apples, mangoes, and bananas, the word "dementia" covers a range of conditions that all share one thing in common — the brain is being damaged in ways that rob a person of their ability to think, remember, and function normally.

The human brain is made up of billions of nerve cells (called neurons) that constantly communicate with each other. In dementia, these neurons get damaged or die, and the connections between them break down. As more and more brain cells are lost, different mental abilities start to fail.

This is not something that happens overnight. It is a progressive condition, meaning it gets worse over time, slowly but steadily.

Dementia affects several areas of mental functioning. The most important ones are:

Memory — This is usually the first and most obvious sign. A person begins forgetting recent events, conversations, and names. They may ask the same question repeatedly, not realizing they already asked it minutes ago. Importantly, they tend to forget recent things while older memories (from childhood or early adulthood) may remain surprisingly intact — at least in the early stages.

Thinking and reasoning — The person struggles to solve problems, plan ahead, or make decisions. Something as routine as managing a household budget or following a recipe becomes difficult or impossible.

Language — They may forget common words, struggle to find the right word mid-sentence, or have trouble following a conversation. They might say "that thing you write with" instead of "pen."

Orientation — They lose track of time, dates, and places. They may not know what year it is, or they may walk out of their home and become lost in a neighbourhood they have lived in for decades.

Judgment — Poor decision-making becomes common. They might dress inappropriately for the weather, hand money to strangers, or be easily cheated.

Personality and behaviour — Perhaps one of the most painful aspects for families: the person may change in character. A calm person may become irritable and aggressive. A social person may become withdrawn. They may develop suspicion, paranoia, or hallucinations (seeing or hearing things that aren't there).

Dementia is caused by diseases or conditions that damage brain tissue. The most common causes have specific names:

Alzheimer's disease is responsible for roughly 60–70% of all dementia cases. In Alzheimer's, abnormal protein deposits (called plaques and tangles) build up inside the brain, slowly destroying neurons.

Vascular dementia is the second most common type. It happens when blood flow to parts of the brain is blocked or reduced — often after a stroke or a series of small strokes — causing brain tissue to die from lack of oxygen.

Lewy body dementia is caused by abnormal deposits of a protein called alpha-synuclein inside brain cells. People with this type often experience hallucinations and movement problems similar to Parkinson's disease.

Frontotemporal dementia affects the front and side parts of the brain (the areas controlling personality, behaviour, and language). It tends to appear at a younger age than other types.

There are over a hundred other, rarer causes of dementia as well. In many cases, a person may have more than one type occurring simultaneously.
Who gets it — and who doesn't

Dementia mainly affects older people. The risk increases significantly with age — it is rare before 65, but after that, the risk roughly doubles every five years.

However — and this is crucial — dementia is not a normal part of ageing. Most old people do not get dementia. Growing old naturally brings some slowdown in thinking and some mild forgetfulness (taking a moment longer to recall a name, for example). That is normal and is not dementia. Dementia is a disease process, not an inevitable consequence of living long.
The difference between normal forgetfulness and dementia

This is a very common confusion, so it deserves its own explanation.

Normal forgetfulness: You forget where you put your keys but remember later. You momentarily forget someone's name but recall it after a while.

Dementia: You forget that you even own keys. You forget who that person is entirely. You forget that you already had lunch and insist you haven't eaten. The forgetting is persistent, worsening, and begins to disrupt the flow of daily life.

The key test is this: Does the memory or thinking problem interfere with the person's ability to live independently? If yes, it is a sign of dementia, not just normal ageing.

Dementia follows a general pattern of early, middle, and late stages, though the speed varies from person to person.

In the early stage, the person may seem mostly fine but begins showing forgetfulness, mild confusion, and some difficulty with complex tasks. They can still live largely independently.

In the middle stage, problems become more obvious and disruptive. The person needs help with daily activities like cooking, bathing, and dressing. They may wander, get confused about people they know, and show significant personality changes.

In the late stage, the person loses the ability to communicate, recognize loved ones, or care for themselves in any way. They are entirely dependent on others. Eventually, the body's most basic functions also fail.

As of now, dementia has no cure. Most types cannot be reversed or stopped. Certain medications and therapies can slow the progression slightly or manage some of the symptoms (such as anxiety, sleep problems, or aggression), but they do not fix the underlying damage.

This makes early detection important — not because it can be cured, but because planning care, making legal and financial arrangements, and getting support early improves the quality of life for both the person and their family.
How to use the word correctly

Dementia is a noun. Some correct ways to use it:

  • "Her doctor diagnosed her with dementia after a series of tests."
  • "Dementia is one of the leading causes of disability among the elderly worldwide."
  • "He was showing early signs of dementia — forgetting appointments and getting confused at home."
  • "There are several types of dementia, with Alzheimer's being the most common."

Note: You say "a person has dementia" or "is living with dementia" — not "is dementia." It describes a condition a person has, not what a person is.
The emotional weight of the word

It is worth knowing that dementia carries deep emotional weight. For families, it often means watching someone they love slowly become a stranger — someone who no longer recognizes them, no longer remembers shared memories, and eventually can no longer function as a person. This is why dementia is often called one of the most devastating conditions in medicine, not just for the person who has it, but for everyone around them.

To understand demerit, you first need to understand merit.

A merit is a good quality — something that makes a person or thing valuable, praiseworthy, or worthy of approval. Think of it as a point in favour of something.

A demerit is the exact opposite. It is a fault, flaw, or disadvantage — something that makes a person or thing less good, less worthy, or less desirable. Think of it as a point against something.

The prefix "de-" signals reversal or removal. So a demerit literally removes or works against merit.

"Demerit" is used in two distinct situations. Both share the same core idea — something negative — but in slightly different ways.

Meaning 1: A Fault or Disadvantage (General Use)

In everyday language, a demerit means a shortcoming or weakness of a person, plan, object, idea, or situation. It is something that counts against it when you are evaluating it.

This meaning is often used when you are weighing the pros and cons of something — comparing what is good about it against what is bad.

Examples:

  • "One demerit of this plan is that it will cost too much money."
  • "The new phone has many good features, but its short battery life is a serious demerit."
  • "They discussed the merits and demerits of moving to a new city."

Notice how in the third example, "merits and demerits" are used together as a natural pair — the good points versus the bad points. This is one of the most common ways the word appears in writing.

Key point: In this meaning, a demerit is not a punishment. It is simply an honest observation that something has a negative quality or a downside.

Meaning 2: An Official Mark of Punishment (Institutional Use)

In certain structured environments — such as schools, the military, police academies, driving licence systems, and workplaces — a demerit is an official black mark recorded against a person's name as a consequence of breaking a rule, behaving badly, or performing poorly.

Think of it as a formal strike against you. The institution keeps count. When you accumulate too many demerits, you face a bigger consequence — such as suspension, losing a licence, or even expulsion.

Examples:

  • "The student received a demerit for arriving late to class three times in a row."
  • "In the driving demerit point system, running a red light adds several demerits to your licence."
  • "After getting five demerits, the cadet was suspended from training."

Key point: In this meaning, a demerit is a tool of accountability used by an institution. It is not just an opinion about someone being flawed — it is an official, recorded consequence with real effects.
How to Tell the Two Meanings Apart

The context will almost always make it clear which meaning is being used.

  • If someone is evaluating or comparing something (a proposal, a product, a decision), they mean Meaning 1 — a fault or disadvantage.
  • If someone is talking about a school, a driving record, a military or professional setting, and a person being given or receiving a demerit, they mean Meaning 2 — an official punishment mark.

1. Demerit implies a judgment.
A demerit is not a random misfortune. It implies that something has been found lacking in quality (Meaning 1) or that a person has done something wrong (Meaning 2). There is always an element of negative evaluation attached to the word.

2. One demerit vs. many demerits.
The word can be used in both singular and plural form naturally.

  • "This is a major demerit of the design." (one flaw)
  • "The system assigns demerits for each violation." (multiple marks)

3. "Merits and demerits" is a fixed, common phrase.
You will very often see or hear these two words paired together. This phrase is the equivalent of saying "the good points and the bad points" or "the advantages and the disadvantages." It is widely used in essays, reports, debates, and formal discussions.

  • "Let us consider the merits and demerits of each option before deciding."

4. Demerit is slightly formal.
In casual speech, people are more likely to say "downside," "flaw," "drawback," or "disadvantage" instead of "demerit." The word "demerit" leans more formal — you'll encounter it more in writing, academic discussion, professional settings, or institutional contexts. However, it is not rare or difficult — it is a perfectly standard English word.

5. A demerit is not the same as a mistake.
A mistake is simply an error — something done incorrectly. A demerit carries a slightly stronger weight: it implies the fault is significant enough to count against someone or something in an evaluation or record.

In general useA demerit = a fault, flaw, or disadvantage of something
In institutional useA demerit = an official punishment mark given to a person
Common phrase"Merits and demerits" = the good points and the bad points
ToneSlightly formal
OppositeMerit
One Final Way to Remember It

Imagine a scoreboard with two columns: one for good points (merits) and one for bad points (demerits). Every time something positive is noted, a merit goes in the first column. Every time something negative is noted — whether it's a flaw in a plan or a rule broken by a person — a demerit goes in the second column.

That image captures both meanings of the word perfectly: a demerit is always something that belongs in the negative column.

Demesne means land that someone holds and uses directly for themselves — not land they rent out or hand over to others, but land they personally possess, control, and occupy as their own.

Think of it this way: if you own a large estate and you farm part of it yourself, live on part of it, and keep the rest as your private grounds, that entire portion under your direct personal control is your demesne. The moment you lease a chunk of it to a tenant farmer and let him work it, that part steps outside your demesne. The demesne is the land that stays in your own hands.
The Feudal World Where This Word Lives

To truly understand demesne, you need to picture the medieval feudal system, because that is where this word was born and where it does most of its work.

In medieval Europe, land was everything — it was wealth, power, and food all at once. A great lord (say, a baron or a king) owned vast stretches of land. But he didn't use all of it himself. He would divide much of it out among lesser lords, knights, and peasant farmers, each of whom would owe him obligations in return — military service, a share of the harvest, taxes, and so on. This granted-out land was not his demesne.

But the lord always kept a core portion back. He worked it with his own servants and serfs, drew its produce directly into his own barns, and kept direct authority over every inch of it. This was his demesne — his home farm, his private reserve, the land that was truly and completely his in a practical, hands-on sense.

So in feudal terms, demesne draws a sharp line between two kinds of land ownership: land you hold "in your own hands" (demesne), and land you've passed down to someone beneath you in the feudal chain. The demesne was always the lord's personal heartland.

In property law — especially old English common law — demesne carries a very precise meaning that grows directly out of that feudal idea.

To hold land "in demesne" means to hold it as the true, direct owner — not through any superior lord, not as a tenant of someone else, but as the actual possessor with the full bundle of ownership rights. You'll sometimes encounter the legal phrase "seised in demesne as of fee," which is one of the most classic expressions in old property law. "Seised" means legally possessed; "in demesne" means as direct owner; "as of fee" means with a permanent, heritable ownership right. Put together, it means: this person owns this land outright, holds it personally, and can pass it on to their heirs.

This legal phrase was the gold standard of land ownership in English law for centuries. If you were seised in demesne as of fee, nobody was above you in the chain — the land was yours in the fullest possible sense.
The "Ancient Demesne" — A Special Legal Category

One specific phrase you may encounter is "ancient demesne." This refers to land that was once held directly by the English Crown — specifically, land recorded as royal land in the Domesday Book of 1086 (the great land survey commissioned by William the Conqueror after he invaded England). Even if that land had since passed into private hands, its history as former Crown land gave it a special legal status. People who held land classed as ancient demesne were entitled to certain old privileges and protections that ordinary landholders didn't enjoy. Courts took this classification seriously for centuries.

Over time, demesne extended beyond its strict feudal and legal homes and came to mean, more generally, any landed estate or the grounds immediately surrounding a manor house or great country house — the private land that belongs to and is enjoyed by the owner of the property. In this looser sense, when a novelist or historian writes about a grand English estate, they might refer to "the demesne" to mean the entire sweep of private grounds — gardens, fields, woods — that belong to the house and its owner.

In an even broader, more figurative sense, demesne is used to mean a person's domain, realm, or sphere of authority — the territory (literal or metaphorical) over which someone holds power. A scientist might be said to work "within the demesne of physics." A judge's demesne is the law. In this usage it functions almost as a synonym for "domain" or "province," with the added sense of personal ownership and control.
The Single Thread Running Through All Meanings

No matter which sense you encounter — feudal, legal, or figurative — the constant core of demesne is this: direct, personal possession and control. It is always about land or territory that belongs to someone in a real, hands-on way, without an intermediary, without being parceled off to others. It is the opposite of delegated or distributed ownership. Whatever is your demesne is truly, immediately, and personally yours.
